lessons.title: Preparing the house for day-old chicks
lessons.html:
Preparing the house for day-old chicks

Brooding is the care of chicks in their first weeks, when they cannot keep themselves warm. Day-old chicks need heat, water, feed and fresh air from the moment they arrive. Mistakes in the first week cause poor growth and deaths that cannot be fixed later.

Before the chicks arrive

  1. The house must be cleaned, disinfected and rested.
  2. Spread clean, dry litter, such as wood shavings, evenly on the floor.
  3. Set up brooder guards (rings) if the farm uses them, to keep chicks near the heat.
  4. Check and light the brooders or heaters well before arrival, often the day before, so the litter and floor are warm. Follow the farm's brooding guide for the target temperature.
  5. Fill drinkers and chick fonts with clean water so it is not ice cold when chicks arrive.
  6. Put out chick feed on paper or in chick trays near the drinkers and heat.
  7. Check lights, curtains, fans and alarms.
  8. Make sure there is enough fuel or gas for the brooding period.

Receiving the chicks

  • Count the boxes and check the delivery note.
  • Off-load quickly. Do not leave boxes in the sun or wind.
  • Place chicks gently near water and feed. Do not drop or throw chicks.
  • Remove weak or dead chicks and record them.
  • Leave the chicks to settle, then check them after a short time.

Gas brooder safety

Check gas pipes and connections for leaks with soapy water, never with a flame. Keep the house ventilated, because heaters use oxygen and can make carbon monoxide. Keep litter and paper away from flames.

lessons.title: Watching chicks and managing heat
lessons.html:
Watching chicks and managing heat

Read the chicks

A thermometer helps, but the chicks show you if the temperature is right. Look at how they spread out.

What you seeMeaningAction
Chicks evenly spread, active, chirping softlyTemperature rightKeep it
Chicks huddled under the heater, loud chirpingToo coldReport and add heat
Chicks far from heater, panting, wings outToo hotReport and reduce heat or ventilate
Chicks crowded to one sideDraught or uneven heatCheck curtains and heaters

Crop check

After some hours, gently feel the crop (at the front of the chest) of a few chicks. A soft, full crop means the chick found feed and water. An empty crop means it did not. Tell your supervisor if many crops are empty.

Daily care in brooding

  • Check birds often in the first days, including at night.
  • Keep drinkers and feeders full and clean. Raise them as chicks grow.
  • Remove dead chicks and record them every day.
  • Keep litter dry. Replace wet patches.
  • Lower the temperature step by step as chicks grow, following the brooding guide.
  • Widen brooder rings as chicks need more space, then remove them.
  • Give fresh air while keeping chicks warm. Ammonia smell means more ventilation is needed.

Records

Record daily temperatures, deaths, feed and water used, and any vaccinations. These records show if brooding is going well.

Key points

  • Warm the house and litter before chicks arrive.
  • Place chicks gently near water and feed straight away.
  • Chick spread shows if the temperature is right.
  • Check crops to see that chicks are eating and drinking.
  • Check gas brooders for leaks with soapy water, never a flame.
  • Lower heat gradually and record everything daily.

quiz.question: Chicks are huddled under the heater and chirping loudly. What does this mean?
Why are brooders lit before the chicks arrive?

options.text: So the litter and floor are warm

quiz.question: A chick has a soft, full crop. What does this tell you?

options.text: It has found feed and water

quiz.question: How should you check a gas brooder for leaks?

options.text: By smelling the pipe closely for a long time
By turning the gas up high

quiz.question: Chicks are far from the heater, panting with wings out. What should happen?

options.text: Report it and reduce heat or ventilate

quiz.question: Boxes of chicks may be left in the sun while you prepare the house.
The brooding temperature is lowered step by step as chicks grow.
What must be ready before day-old chicks arrive? (select all that apply)
